Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in this domain, particularly in automating the process of hypothesis generation-a core component of scientific discovery. This paper explores the current capabilities and methodologies of AI systems designed to formulate plausible, testable scientific hypotheses by synthesizing patterns, identifying anomalies, and integrating multi-domain knowledge. \"info:eu-repo/semantics/article\"}, \"abstract\": \"The integration of Artificial Intelligence into scientific discovery represents a paradigm shift in how research is conducted across disciplines. This study investigates the effectiveness of AI-driven automation in accelerating and enhancing scientific discovery through a mixed-methods design combining quantitative performance analysis with qualitative expert evaluation. Using datasets from materials science, fluid dynamics, and autonomous experimentation platforms, we examined how AI systems—including large language models, autonomous agents, and self-driving laboratories—perform across the scientific workflow from hypothesis generation to experimental execution and knowledge dissemination. Quantitative results demonstrate that AI-driven autonomous experimentation significantly increases the diversity of explored phenomena compared to conventional optimization routines, with novelty discovery scores improving by up to 31% over traditional approaches. AI agent frameworks successfully automated the complete research cycle, including hypothesis generation, experimental design, robotic execution, data analysis, and manuscript preparation, reducing research cycle time by approximately 60% in well-defined domains. However, qualitative findings revealed that AI systems face persistent challenges in identifying conceptual gaps that require structural insight beyond existing knowledge frameworks. Expert evaluation indicated that while AI excels at search, optimization, and pattern recognition, human researchers remain essential for formulating fundamentally novel research directions and providing interpretive judgment. These findings contribute to a nuanced understanding of AI’s role in scientific discovery and provide practical guidelines for designing human-AI collaborative research systems that balance automation with scientific creativity.\"}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "0eacbd8d5b24ffd10a7aae54e17aaf2fde5ee928f37dafdcb7aa32c88db9243d", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unassigned_problem", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.1038/s42254-022-00518-3", "doi:10.22541/au.175044376.61922933/v1", "doi:10.3386/w31558", "openalex:W4304185479", "openalex:W4411483653", "openalex:W4385804359", "openalex:W7217506496"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.1038/s42254-022-00518-3", "https://pure.mpg.de/rest/items/item_3450670/component/file_3450671/content", "https://doi.org/10.22541/au.175044376.61922933/v1", "https://doi.org/10.3386/w31558"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

Risk-aware DRL methods now incorporate volatility, drawdown, and tail risk constraints directly into the reward or optimization objective, while multiobjective frameworks enable fine-grained control of risk/return trade-offs across diverse investors [Lwele et al., 2025, Deng et al., 2024]. In options and volatility trading, multi-agent architectures that separate the decision to take risk from the policy used to hedge it have been shown to improve risk-adjusted performance relative to traditional or single-agent baselines [Bańka and Chudziak, 2025, Chen et al., 2025]. At the same time, explainable AI (XAI) techniques and sentimentaware tail risk models demonstrate that interpretable drivers of risk can be extracted and communicated to portfolio managers and risk committees [Exp, 2023, Klinkert, 2024]. This paper surveys these developments and proposes a research agenda for autonomous portfolio and derivatives risk management agents that (i) monitor Greeks, volatility regime shifts, and liquidity, (ii) dynamically hedge multi-asset portfolios, and (iii) use scenario-simulation agents to stress test risk, all under a risk-aware, multi-objective, and explainable decision-making framework. We argue that this niche has strong direct capital allocation implications, is rich in deep quantitative structure, and is a natural fit for combining RL with LLM-based reasoning, making it highly relevant to hedge funds and systematic trading desks.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6310078\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.20944/preprints202503.1966.v1\", \"title\": [\"Intelligent Flight Procedure Design: A Reinforcement Learning Approach with Pareto-Based Multi-Objective Optimization\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Current flight procedure design primarily relies on expert experience, lacking a systematic approach to comprehensively balance safety, route simplification, and environmental impact. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a reinforcement learning-based method that leverages carefully crafted reward engineering to achieve an optimized flight procedure design, effectively considering safety, route simplicity, and environmental friendliness. To further enhance performance by tackling the low sampling efficiency in the Replay Buffer, we introduce a multi-objective sampling strategy based on the Pareto frontier, integrated with the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method generates executable flight procedures in the BlueSky open-source flight simulator, successfully balancing these three conflicting objectives, while achieving a 28.6% increase in convergence speed and a 4% improvement in comprehensive performance across safety, route simplification, and environmental impact compared to the baseline algorithm. This study offers an efficient and validated solution for the intelligent design of flight procedures.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202503.1966.v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025, 3, 26]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "ae8af700273e6fd5dbcafe6b46c3a5299f2f716ada61bd1d047bbf7fa2f80621", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unassigned_objectives", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.4673021", "doi:10.1007/springerreference_72504", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6310078", "doi:10.20944/preprints202503.1966.v1"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4673021", "https://doi.org/10.1007/springerreference_72504", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6310078", "https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202503.1966.v1"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
